deep.reconstruction:
Context. The previous page determines an orbit from two heliocentric places (log a = 0.3728428, a = 2.359624; node 103°8'53.38"; i = 7°5'49.5"). These elements match Vesta, and the margin date is 1810. This page, headed 'Berechnung der Constanten', turns those elements into an ephemeris of heliocentric equatorial rectangular coordinates for 1810 March 29 to May 8 at 4-day steps. The procedure is Gauss's own (Theoria Motus 1809, arts. 56-58), in the variant where the coordinates are written directly as functions of the eccentric anomaly E.

(1) Anomalies and epoch, top left.
- 𝔉 = 297°5'23.74" and f = 3°0'31.18" (f is half of 189°13'53.00" - 183°12'50.64" from the previous page).
- True anomalies: v = 𝔉 - f = 294°4'52.56" and v' = 𝔉 + f = 300°5'54.92".
- Eccentric anomalies: 𝔊 = 301°57'28.14" and g = 2°52'1.544", so E = 𝔊 - g = 299°5'26.596" and E' = 𝔊 + g = 304°49'29.684".
- Kepler's equation M = E - e'' sin E, with e'' = e·206264.8".
  - log e = 8.9890276, e = 0.0975052, log e'' = 4.3034527.
  - log|sin E| = 9.9414374 and log|sin E'| = 9.9142908.
  - e''|sin E| = 4°52'54.79" and e''|sin E'| = 4°35'9.863".
  - Hence m = 303°58'21.386" and m' = 309°24'39.547".
- m' - m = 5°26'18.161" in 20 days (Mar 29 to Apr 18). So the daily motion is 978.908" (cf. '978 9091' on the previous page), and the 4-day motion is 1°5'15.63".
- Perihelion: π = 183°12'50.64" - v = 249°7'58.08" (aphelion 69°7'58.08").
- Mean longitudes: L = m + π = 193°6'19.466" (Mar 29, 9h) and m' + π = 198°32'37.63" (written .625). At 12h: 193°8'21.83" (+3h × 978.908"/24 = 122.36").
- Argument of perihelion: ω = π - Ω = 145°59'4.70" (hence the note 'v + 145°59'…', i.e. u = v + ω), with Ω = 103°8'53.38".

(2) Gaussian constants, columns 3-6. The defining relations are:
- sin a sin A = cos Ω; sin a cos A = -cos i sin Ω.
- sin b sin B = cos ε sin Ω; sin b cos B = cos ε cos i cos Ω - sin ε sin i.
- sin c sin C = sin ε sin Ω; sin c cos C = sin ε cos i cos Ω + cos ε sin i.
- Then x = r sin a sin(A+u), y = r sin b sin(B+u), z = r sin c sin(C+u).

Logarithms used:
- log|tan Ω| = 0.6315392, log cos i = 9.9966597, log sin i = 9.0918461, log tan i = 9.0951864.
- log|cos Ω| = 9.3569240, log sin Ω = 9.9884631.
- log cos ε = 9.9625167, log sin ε = 9.6000696, with ε = 23°27'50".

Constant for x:
- cot A = tan Ω cos i (0.6281989), giving A = 193°14'46.00".
- log sin a = 9.3569240 - 9.3600901 = 9.9968338.

Constants for y and z, via an auxiliary angle N:
- tan N = tan i / cos Ω (log 9.7382624n), N = 151°18'21.82", N + ε = 174°46'11.82".
- log(cos i cot Ω) = 9.3651205n; minus log|cos N| (9.9430971) gives 9.4220234n.
- cot B = cos i cot Ω cos(N+ε)/(cos N cos ε): 9.4220234 + 0.0374833 + 9.9981882 = 9.4576949n, so B = 106°0'24.98".
- log sin b = log cos ε + log sin Ω - log sin B = 9.9681533.
- cot C = cos i cot Ω sin(N+ε)/(cos N sin ε): 9.4220234 + 0.3999304 + log sin(N+ε) [= 8.9587799 needed] = 8.7807337, so C = 86°32'16.79".
- log sin c = 9.6000696 + 9.9884631 + 0.0007933 = 9.5893260.

Control via a second auxiliary angle N':
- tan N' = tan i cos Ω (8.4521104n), N' = 178°22'39.91", N' + ε = 201°50'29.91".
- Gauss uses cos i / cos N' = sin a (9.9968338).
- cos a = sin i sin Ω (9.0803092).
- cos b = sin a |sin(N'+ε)|: 9.9968338 + 9.5705926 = 9.5674264.
- cos c = sin a |cos(N'+ε)|: 9.9968338 + 9.9676489 = 9.9644827.
- These agree with sin b and sin c, a closure check.

(3) Reduction to eccentric anomaly, middle block. Use r cos v = a(cos E - e) and r sin v = a cos φ sin E, with log cos φ = 9.9979256. Then

 x = a sin a [sin(A+ω) cos E + cos φ cos(A+ω) sin E] - a e sin a sin(A+ω) = α sin(A' + E) + γ,

with α sin A' = a sin a sin(A+ω) and α cos A' = a sin a cos φ cos(A+ω). Likewise for y (B', β, δ) and z (C', κ, λ).

Arguments:
- A + ω = 339°13'50.70", B + ω = 251°59'29.68", C + ω = 232°31'21.49".

Logarithms:
- log a sin a = 0.3696766, with cos φ: 0.3676022.
- log a sin b = 0.3409961, with cos φ: 0.3389217.
- log a sin c = 9.9621688, with cos φ: 9.9600944.
- log|sin(A+ω)| = 9.5497451, log|cos(A+ω)| = 9.9708189.
- log|sin(B+ω)| = 9.9781856 and log|cos(B+ω)| = 9.4901788. Gauss crossed out 9.9781582 and 9.4904378 and recomputed.
- log|sin(C+ω)| = 9.8995983, log|cos(C+ω)| = 9.7842234.

Results:
- x: A' = 339°8'23.46", log α = 9.9194217 - log cos-quotient = 0.3678641 (log cos A' = 9.9705572).
- y: tan B' from 0.3191817n and 9.8291005n gives B' = 252°4'18.80"; log sin B' = 9.9783830, so log β = 0.3407987.
- z: log κ = 9.8617671 - 9.9003638 = 9.9614033. This requires C' = 232°39'16.93".

Additive constants γ = -a e sin a sin(A+ω), etc. (sin(A+ω), sin(B+ω), sin(C+ω) are all negative, so all three constants are positive):
- γ = +0.0809933 = 10^(8.9890276 + 9.9194217).
- δ = +0.2033228.
- λ = +0.0709242.
- Older values 0.0810348 and 0.0709737 are struck out.

(4) Ephemeris table.
- Mean anomaly: M_k = 303°58'21.39" + k·1°5'15.63" (k = 0..10).
- E_k is obtained from E = M + e'' sin E. Examples: Mar 29 299°5'26.60", Apr 2 300°14'0.75", Apr 6 301°22'42.19", Apr 26 307°7'56.77", Apr 30 308°17'20.74", May 4 309°26'51.58", May 8 310°36'29.19"; Apr 10-22 are on the next page.
- The column 4.3034527, 9.9414374 … 9.8803443 gives log e'' and log|sin E_k|.
- The three columns give log|sin(A'+E)|, log|sin(B'+E)|, log|sin(C'+E)|.
- The last block gives α sin(A'+E), β sin(B'+E), κ sin(C'+E). For example, Mar 29: -2.3087011, -0.4243175, +0.1313627. The z term changes sign between Apr 22 and Apr 26.
- Adding γ, δ, λ yields x, y, z on the next page; e.g. x(Mar 29) = -2.3087011 + 0.0809933 = -2.2277078.
errors: Mean longitude for the second epoch is written 198°32'37.625"; 309°24'39.547" + 249°7'58.08" = 198°32'37.627". This is a 0.002" rounding slip and is harmless.

Gauss corrected his first values log|sin(B+ω)| = 9.9781582 and log|cos(B+ω)| = 9.4904378 to 9.9781856 and 9.4901788. My recomputation confirms the corrected values. The older block (0.3191543, 9.8293595, 9.9783966) is superseded, and the constants 0.0810348 and 0.0709737 are struck out.

The z auxiliary angle reads 232°39'6.93" in the transcription, but everything downstream requires C' = 232°39'16.93". This includes log sin C' = 9.9003638, log κ = 9.9614033, and the table value log sin(C'+E) = 9.1570687 for Mar 29. So either the manuscript has 16,93 or Gauss wrote a 10" slip that he did not use. The computation itself is consistent.

No substantive mathematical errors found. The checked entries reproduce to about 1 unit in the 7th decimal: log sin E, e'' sin E, M, E, A, sin a, B, sin b, C, sin c, A', α, B', β, κ, γ, δ, λ, and sample table rows.

Next-page sums (x, y, z) partly disagree with this page's components plus constants. For example, -0.4243175 + 0.2033228 = -0.2209947 versus -0.2209967, and 0.1313627 + 0.0709242 = 0.2022869 versus 0.2012869. These are probably transcription errors on the next page, but should be checked against the image.

results.what: Solution of Kepler's equation M = E - e'' sin E for the eccentric anomaly at 4-day steps, with log e'' = 4.3034527 (e = 0.0975052).

Gaussian constants for heliocentric equatorial coordinates: sin a, A, sin b, B, sin c, C, with x = r sin a sin(A+u) etc. Computed with auxiliary angles N and N', and checked via cos a = sin i sin Ω and cos b, cos c.
results.modern_name: Gaussian vectorial/equatorial constants (P, Q orientation vectors in polar form)

results.what: Coordinates written as harmonic functions of the eccentric anomaly: x = α sin(A'+E) + γ, with α sin A' = a sin a sin(A+ω), α cos A' = a sin a √(1-e²) cos(A+ω), γ = -a e sin a sin(A+ω).
results.modern_name: Ephemeris computation via eccentric anomaly (x = a P_x (cos E - e) + b Q_x sin E)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss / standard 19th-century ephemeris practice (Encke and others)

results.what: Ephemeris of heliocentric equatorial coordinates of Vesta for 1810 Mar 29 to May 8, as working material for comparison with observations (Bode's are on the next page).
results.usually_credited_to: Routine astronomical practice; Gauss was known to compute minor-planet ephemerides

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine working application of the methods Gauss published in Theoria Motus (1809), used to make an ephemeris of Vesta in 1810. It is of value as documentation of his computing practice: the auxiliary-angle checks and his self-corrections. It contains nothing mathematically new.
